name: Staghorn Coral
description: Fast-growing antler-like branches that once forested Caribbean reefs. Staghorn thickets shelter juvenile fish and break wave energy. Look — never touch — the branches snap easily and cuts heal slowly.
funFact: Staghorn rarely reproduces by eggs alone — broken fragments re-attach and regrow, which restoration divers exploit to rebuild reefs.
imageCredit:
Albert Kok at Dutch Wikipedia

(Original text: albert kok)

name: Elkhorn Coral
habitat: Shallow reef crests pounded by waves
description: Broad, flattened branches like moose antlers, forming shallow reef barriers where snorkellers most often see them. Their decline from disease and bleaching transformed Caribbean coastlines.
funFact: Elkhorn's flat shape evolved to catch light in shallow surf — entire reefs grow sideways into the sun.

name: Table Coral
description: Broad horizontal plates that shade the reef below and shade-hunt beneath them. Snorkellers drifting over a reef flat see them like dinner tables set for dinner — each one a city of fish.
funFact: A single table coral can host several species of territorial damselfish gardening their own algal lawns on it.

name: Grooved Brain Coral
description: Smooth domes folded like a brain's surface. Their slow growth — millimetres a year — builds reef foundations that outlive centuries.
funFact: The maze-like ridges channel mucus and trapped food toward the polyp mouths running down each valley.

name: Pillar Coral
habitat: Flat reef areas and sandy patches
description: Distinctive finger-like pillars standing from the seabed. During the day its polyps stay hidden; snorkellers who visit at dusk see the pillars 'fuzzy' with extended tentacles.
funFact: It's one of the few corals whose polyps are extended during daylight — earning the nickname 'fingers of the reef'.

name: Boulder Star Coral
description: The Caribbean's reef-building workhorse: massive boulder colonies of knobbly, star-shaped corallites. It grows so slowly that large boulders are centuries old.
funFact: Boulder star coral rings, like tree rings, let scientists read centuries of ocean climate history.

name: Finger Coral
description: Pale lilac or tan fingers clustered in cushions. It tolerates murky, warm water that other corals reject, so snorkellers see it even in degraded lagoons.
funFact: Some Porites colonies in the Pacific have been growing for over 1,000 years — among the oldest animals alive.

name: Fire Coral
description: Despite the name, fire coral is a hydrocoral, not a true coral. Its yellow-brown branches deliver a fierce burning sting on contact. Watch for it in surge zones — wear a rash guard if you're prone to contact.
funFact: The sting comes from millions of microscopic stinging nematocysts that fire a tiny harpoon into your skin on touch.

name: Sea Fan
description: Flat, lattice-like fans that strain plankton from passing currents. Purple sea fans are flexible — unlike hard corals, they bend with the surge instead of breaking.
funFact: Sea fans orient across the current like solar panels — each new branch grows into the food-bearing flow.

name: Leather Coral
description: Soft corals shaped like leather toadstools; the surface flushes with polyps at night to feed. They lack the hard skeleton of reef-building corals, so they sway in the current.
funFact: Leather corals wage chemical warfare — they release compounds that stunt neighbouring corals competing for space.

name: Carnation Coral
habitat: Walls and overhangs with strong current
description: Impossibly vivid pink, orange and violet soft corals that glow on deep reef walls. They feed on passing plankton, so they thrive where currents bring food.
funFact: Their neon colours come from proteins in the skin — related to the GFP that makes jellyfish glow in labs.

name: Bubble Coral
description: By day it looks like a cluster of translucent grapes; by night the bubbles deflate and tentacles sweep the water for food. It's one of the reef's odder-looking residents.
funFact: The bubbles are inflated water-filled vesicles that act as built-in sunglasses for the coral below.

name: Organ Pipe Coral
description: A skeleton of deep-red vertical tubes, each occupied by a single polyp — unmistakable and beautiful. It forms carpets of pipes connected by horizontal runways.
funFact: The vivid red skeleton is exposed where the polyps retract, making this one of the most collected corals — legally protected in many countries.

name: Mushroom Coral
description: A single free-living polyp shaped like a dinner plate, lying loose on the sand. Unlike most corals, it doesn't need to stay attached — it can even right itself when flipped.
funFact: One mushroom coral is a single animal — not a colony — and it can slowly crawl using its tentacles.

name: Cauliflower Coral
description: Stubby, domed branches with a bumpy surface, usually tinted pink, brown or lavender. Its dense thickets are nurseries for small fish and shrimp that shelter between the knobs.
funFact: Some damselfish 'farm' cauliflower coral by biting the tips — pruning it into lollipop shapes to suit their gardens.

name: Magnificent Sea Anemone
habitat: Reef tops and slopes in clear light
description: Enormous purple-tipped tents, often carpeted with clownfish. The anemone hosts the fish in exchange for scraps and defence — one of nature's most iconic partnerships.
funFact: Some anemones slowly walk the reef on their basal disc when their spot gets too shady — a journey of centimetres per month.

name: Blue Coral
description: Its skeleton is genuinely blue — iron salts in the tissue tint the colony a smoky steel-blue — with pale brown polyps. It is a 'living fossil', unchanged for 100+ million years.
funFact: Blue coral is the sole surviving species of its entire order — the last member of a lineage older than the dinosaurs.

name: Black Coral
description: Living tissue comes in greens, yellows and whites — the jet-black skeleton only shows when polished. Slow-growing and long-lived, black corals are protected nearly everywhere they occur.
funFact: Radiocarbon dating has found Hawaiian black corals over 4,000 years old — the oldest marine animals known.
imageCredit: Image courtesy of Dr. Scott France.

name: Red Gorgonian
description: The Mediterranean's signature sea fan — crimson branches forming forests on dim rocky walls where little else grows. They filter plankton from the cool currents.
funFact: Red gorgonian forests shelter seahorses and neon-red shrimp that live nowhere else in the Mediterranean.

name: Massive Porites
description: Lemon-yellow or green boulders, some of the largest coral colonies on Earth. Snorkellers in Hawaii and the Great Barrier Reef swim past 'Porites cities' that took a millennium to grow.
funFact: The largest known Porites colony in American Samoa is over 5 m tall and estimated to be more than 800 years old.

name: Rose Coral
description: A small, elliptical coral like a rose fossil, often found loose in the grass beds. Like mushroom coral, young colonies live loose on the sand and can even move with the waves.
funFact: Rose corals can right themselves after storms flip them over — by inflating one side and shifting weight.

name: Open Brain Coral
habitat: Sandy and rubble bottoms beside reefs
description: A single, fleshy polyp that inflates into wavy folds of green, red and brown, looking like a brain left on the sand. Its valleys and ridges feed mucus toward the mouth at the centre. Unlike reef-building corals, it often lives loose on soft bottoms.
funFact: Open brain corals can inflate their tissue with water to cover sharp rubble beneath them — their own built-in cushion.

name: Elegance Coral
habitat: Muddy reef flats, lagoons and seagrass edges
description: Long, flowing tentacles with glowing green tips spread from a fleshy, sand-dwelling colony. The elegance coral is one of the few large corals that tolerates silty inshore water, but its stinging cells still demand space from neighbours and from snorkellers.
funFact: Its common name comes from the way the tentacles sway like a ballgown in the current — but that skirt carries a powerful sting.

name: Torch Coral
description: Clusters of long, tubular tentacles tipped with pale, glowing bulbs — like a bank of torches swaying in the surge. Torch corals are popular in aquariums, which has increased pressure on wild colonies. Their tentacles deliver a sharp sting to bare skin.
funFact: At night they extend longer sweeper tentacles to sting and clear space from neighbouring corals.

name: Hammer Coral
description: Tentacles shaped like tiny hammers or anchors, coloured green, pink or gold. Hammer corals grow in dense clusters on sheltered reef slopes and expand their tentacles to feed at night. Every one of those hammers is loaded with stinging cells.
funFact: Each hammer-shaped tentacle can act like a slow, muscular hand, passing food along to the mouth at the colony's centre.

name: Pulsing Xenia Coral
habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and shallow rubble
description: Soft corals that spread in soft, feathered mats, their eight-tentacled polyps opening and closing in a slow, hypnotic pulse. Xenia thrives on shallow, nutrient-rich reef flats and can colonise rubble quickly after a storm.
funFact: The pulsing rhythm varies with current and light, and may help the colony exchange water for feeding and oxygen.

name: Green Star Polyps
habitat: Reef rubble, walls and shallow rocky patches
description: A purple or maroon encrusting mat from which bright green, star-shaped polyps emerge like a field of tiny flowers. Green star polyps spread quickly over bare rock and rubble, making them both a reef pioneer and a nuisance to neighbouring corals.
funFact: They are soft corals that produce a tough, rubbery mat instead of a stony skeleton — flexible enough to survive surge.

name: Giant Clam
habitat: Shallow reef flats and sandy lagoon patches
description: The largest living bivalve, with a thick, fluted shell and a mantle striped in blue, green and gold. Giant clams farm algae inside their tissues, giving them energy from sunlight. They grow slowly and live for decades, so they are vulnerable to harvesting.
funFact: A giant clam cannot snap shut fast enough to trap a diver — the old myth of being held underwater by a clam is just a story.

name: Crown-of-thorns Starfish
habitat: Coral reefs, especially once dense coral cover builds up
description: A many-armed starfish covered in venomous spines, feeding by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and digesting coral alive. In outbreaks it can strip a reef bare. The spines break off in skin and cause a painful, burning wound — look, never touch.
funFact: A single female can release tens of millions of eggs in a spawning season, which helps trigger the outbreaks that plague some reefs.

name: Christmas Tree Worm
habitat: Embedded in coral heads, especially Porites
description: Two spiral crowns of feathery tentacles spiralling out of a coral head, often in red, blue or yellow. The worm lives in a tube it has bored into the coral and retreats in a blink if a shadow passes overhead. It filters plankton from the current.
funFact: Each crown is a specialised feeding and breathing structure — the rest of the worm stays hidden in its coral burrow its whole life.

name: Great Star Coral
habitat: Reef slopes, walls and shaded overhangs
description: A massive Caribbean coral whose large, star-shaped polyps stay open in daylight — an unusual sight on a reef. Colonies can be domes, plates or columns, and the polyps come in shades of green, brown and orange. It is a resilient reef builder.
funFact: Unlike many corals, great star coral is often seen feeding during the day, its polyps stretched out like tiny sea anemones.

name: Zoanthid
habitat: Shallow reef flats, rocks and rubble
description: Colourful colonial polyps that carpet rocks like tiny daisies, often green, orange or electric blue. They look soft and harmless, but some zoanthids carry palytoxin, one of the most potent natural toxins known. Never handle, taste or scrub them.
funFact: Palytoxin from zoanthids is so potent that aquarium hobbyists have been hospitalised simply from fumes released while cleaning a tank.

name: Mustard Hill Coral
diet: Plankton and nutrients from symbiotic algae
description: A lumpy, mustard-yellow coral made of tightly packed bumps. It is one of the toughest Caribbean corals and can survive in murky or wave-washed shallows where other corals struggle.
funFact: Mustard hill coral broods its larvae, releasing ready-to-settle young instead of broadcast eggs.

name: Lettuce Coral
diet: Plankton and nutrients from symbiotic algae
description: Overlapping leaf-like plates with radiating ridges, often in shades of brown, purple or green. The plates grow at different angles to catch light on slopes and in shaded overhangs.
funFact: Its upright plates work like solar panels, spreading to catch sunlight at different depths.

name: Giant Barrel Sponge
diet: Bacteria and plankton filtered from seawater
description: A huge brown barrel-shaped sponge with a wide opening at the top. It pumps seawater through its body, filtering out bacteria and plankton, and can dominate deeper Caribbean reef slopes.
funFact: Some giant barrel sponges are estimated to be centuries old.

name: Long-spined Sea Urchin
habitat: Reef flats, seagrass beds and rubble
description: A black urchin with extremely long, brittle spines that can deliver painful wounds. It grazes algae and shelters in crevices during the day, playing a big role in keeping Caribbean reefs from being overgrown.
funFact: A mass die-off in the 1980s removed most of these urchins and helped algae smother many reefs.

name: Flower Coral
description: Clusters of tubular corallites with pale centres and brown walls, looking like small flowers. It extends its tentacles at night to catch plankton and often grows in shaded overhangs.
funFact: It is a slow-growing coral that can persist in low light where many other corals cannot.
imageCredit: Photographer: Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary Staff

name: Blade Fire Coral
description: Upright blade-like plates with a smooth, pale surface, often forming dense thickets on shallow reef crests. Despite the name and appearance, it is a hydrozoan, not a true stony coral.
funFact: Its stinging cells are tiny but can leave a painful, itchy rash on bare skin.

name: Encrusting Gorgonian
habitat: Reef walls, rubble and shaded ledges
description: A purple-brown soft coral that spreads as a rubbery mat over rock and rubble. Its pale polyps emerge to feed at night, and the mat can overgrow nearby corals and sponges.
funFact: It grows outward as a sheet rather than building upright branches.

name: Black Sea Fan
description: A dark, bushy gorgonian with thin flexible branches, usually found on deeper walls and drop-offs. Its polyps open at night to strain plankton from the current.
funFact: Its skeleton is flexible and dark, unlike the hard white skeleton of stony corals.

name: Montipora Coral
diet: Plankton and nutrients from symbiotic algae
description: A fast-growing coral with finger-like branches in brown, purple or green. It is one of the most widespread reef-builders in the Indo-Pacific and provides shelter for small fish and crustaceans.
funFact: Montipora corals can grow quickly but are sensitive to bleaching and disease.
imageCredit: No machine-readable author provided. Haplochromis assumed (based on copyright claims).

name: Duncan Coral
description: A colonial coral with tubular corallites and greenish tentacles, often forming small clumps on sandy reef edges. Each polyp has its own mouth but shares a skeleton with its neighbours.
funFact: Its common name comes from the Duncan family, early collectors of the species.

name: Scolymia Coral
description: A solitary, fleshy coral with a round shape and prominent ridges. It comes in many colours and can capture surprisingly large food items with its tentacles.
funFact: Some Scolymia corals can swallow small fish and shrimp whole.

name: Blue Sea Star
description: A bright blue starfish with long, rounded arms, often seen on reef flats and rubble. It moves slowly over the bottom, feeding on algae and detritus, and can regrow lost arms.
funFact: It can regenerate not just an arm but an entire body from a fragment.

name: Bubble-tip Anemone
description: A sea anemone with tentacles that often end in bulbous tips, usually brown, green or pink. It hosts several clownfish species and can retract into a crevice when disturbed.
funFact: The bulbous tips may help the anemone capture food and shelter its clownfish partners.

name: Small Giant Clam
diet: Sunlight via symbiotic algae, plus plankton
habitat: Shallow reef flats and coral heads
description: A colourful clam that embeds itself in coral or rock, exposing a mantle full of symbiotic algae. It can close its shell quickly when shadowed, and is much smaller than the true giant clam.
funFact: Its mantle can be brilliant blue, green or purple thanks to the algae living inside it.

name: Sinularia Coral
description: A soft leathery coral with finger-like lobes that sway in the current. It sheds mucus to clean itself and can release chemicals that discourage neighbouring corals from growing too close.
funFact: Soft corals like this have no hard stony skeleton, only tiny flexible spicules.

name: Mediterranean Cup Coral
habitat: Shallow rocky reefs and seagrass edges
description: Clusters of brown, cup-shaped corallites that build small banks in shallow Mediterranean water. It is one of the few reef-building corals in the Mediterranean and is vulnerable to heat waves.
funFact: Its colonies can grow large enough to be considered a true reef.

name: Red Coral
habitat: Dark caves and deep rocky walls
description: A slow-growing gorgonian with a bright red skeleton and white polyps, living in shaded caves and deep walls. It has been harvested for jewellery for thousands of years and is now heavily depleted in many areas.
funFact: Some red coral colonies are thought to live for centuries.

name: Yellow Gorgonian
description: A yellow fan-shaped gorgonian with polyps arranged in rows along its branches. It feeds by catching plankton from the current and is a familiar sight on Mediterranean walls.
funFact: Gorgonians orient their fans across the current to catch the most plankton.

name: Snakelocks Anemone
description: A sea anemone with long, slender green tentacles tipped with purple, often growing in sunlit shallow water. It hosts symbiotic algae and can survive long periods without catching food.
funFact: Its tentacles stay extended in daylight to let the algae inside it photosynthesise.

name: Giant Pavona Coral
diet: Plankton and nutrients from symbiotic algae
description: A massive coral that builds broad plates and mounds, often dominating eastern Pacific reefs. Its surface is covered in small polyps that give it a rough, ridged texture.
funFact: It is one of the main reef-building corals in the tropical eastern Pacific.

name: Orange Coral
description: A solitary orange cup coral that grows on rocky walls and under overhangs along the eastern Pacific coast. It extends translucent tentacles to feed and retracts them when touched.
funFact: It broods its larvae and colonises new rock slowly, one polyp at a time.

name: Orange Cup Coral
habitat: Shaded reef walls, caves and pilings
description: Bright orange tubular polyps that grow in clusters on shaded walls, caves and artificial structures. Unlike many reef corals, it has no symbiotic algae and depends entirely on catching plankton.
funFact: It is a successful invader and can spread on ship hulls and oil platforms.

name: Pacific Sea Fan
description: A golden-brown gorgonian sea fan with a branching, net-like shape, found along the eastern Pacific coast. It grows across the current and feeds on plankton drifting past.
funFact: Sea fans are colonies of tiny polyps, not plants, despite their branch-like appearance.

name: Green Knob Coral
diet: Plankton and nutrients from symbiotic algae
description: Greenish-grey lumpy colonies with small polyps, often found in shaded parts of rocky reefs. It tolerates cooler water than many reef corals and is common in southern Australia.
funFact: It is one of the few reef corals that thrives in the cooler waters of southern Australia.

name: Devonshire Cup Coral
description: A small solitary coral with a cup-shaped skeleton and translucent tentacles tipped in white. It lives on rocky walls and wrecks, often in shaded spots where currents bring plankton.
funFact: Each polyp lives alone rather than in a colony, unlike most reef-building corals.

name: Dead Man's Fingers
habitat: Rocky reefs, wrecks and tide-swept walls
description: A pale soft coral with thick finger-like lobes and white polyps that emerge to feed. It is common on cold-water rocky reefs and wrecks, where it sways in strong currents.
funFact: Its ghostly hand-shaped colonies gave it its common name.
